The Bangor Historical Society’s Ghostly Bangor Walking Tour features tales of unsolved mysteries, murder, and energies that may still linger in the Queen City. Tours stroll through the streets of Downtown Bangor and last around 90 minutes. Tickets are $12.

Advanced ticketing is required. Our tours are capped at 25 guests, and tickets sell out quickly. Tickets must be purchased by noon of the date of the tour. To purchase tickets or for more info please visit our website or e-mail us at curator@bangorhistoricalsociety.org.
Tours depart from the Bangor Historical Society’s Thomas A. Hill House (159 Union Street, Bangor) at 7 p.m. Parking is available on High Street.

A note on inclement weather: tours will be cancelled if there is a chance of thunderstorms but not if only rain is in the forecast.

Saturday, October 3 | 6:00–9:00 PM
Penobscot Valley Country Club
366 Main Street, Orono

Join the Bangor Historical Society for Liberty & Legacy: BHS Annual Awards Night, an evening celebrating those who have made a lasting impact on our community and its history, while commemorating the 250th anniversary of the United States and the Declaration of Independence.

Guests are invited to embrace the spirit of the evening by dressing in patriotic colors or as a favorite historical figure. The celebration will include a buffet-style dinner, the presentation of the Bangor Historical Society’s annual awards, and a special opportunity to experience a remarkable piece of American history.
2026 Award Honorees
George Hale
Judge John E. Godfrey Eye Witness to History Award
Bangor Savings Bank
Founding Fathers Preservation & Stewardship Award
Michael Pullen, AIA, LEED AP, Artifex Architects & Engineers
Nelson E. Durgin Generations of Service Award

In honor of this historic milestone, the Bangor Historical Society’s rare William Stone engraving of the Declaration of Independence will make a special trip to Orono and be on display for guests during the evening.
Tickets
Individual: $75
Couple: $140
Table of 8: $560
We hope you’ll join us on October 3 for a memorable evening celebrating history, preservation, service, and the people who help keep our shared stories alive.

Thank you to our sponsors:  Cross Insurance & The City of Bangor.

Explore Bangor’s dark side and take a walk amid the shadows during the Bangor Historical Society’s Darker Mount Hope Cemetery Tour, Friday and Saturday, October 23 & 24, 2026.

As the night deepens while you meander the paved paths, a cast of living souls will regale you with dramatic, moving, touching, mysterious, and even spooky stories —sprinkled with a bit of history, of course— about the permanent residents of Mount Hope. This nighttime walking tour of one of the oldest garden cemeteries in the country is a seasonal favorite.
<div>

Tours are conducted on foot and are no more than one mile, but may include stairs, hills, and uneven terrain. We recommend sturdy footwear, warm clothing, and a flashlight. Tours are conducted rain or shine.
<div>
Advanced Tickets are required and are sold for specific start times, starting at 6 pm.
<div>
<div>
Tickets will go on sale to the public on Thursday, September 24th, at noon.
<div>

Guests should enter Mount Hope Cemetery at 1048 State Street, Bangor, and check in near the Superintendent’s Lodge at no sooner than 20 minutes before their departure time. Parking is available along both sides of the cemetery entry road, accessible via the State Street gate.
<div>
Use “Second Maine Regiment Memorial” into GPS for the correct entrance gate location.
<div>
Direct questions to the museum curator via email at curator@bangorhistoricalsociety.org or by calling 207-942-1900.

Explore Bangor’s dark side and take a walk amid the shadows during the Bangor Historical Society’s Darker Mount Hope Cemetery Tour, Friday and Saturday, October 23 & 24, 2026.

As the night deepens while you meander the paved paths, a cast of living souls will regale you with dramatic, moving, touching, mysterious, and even spooky stories —sprinkled with a bit of history, of course— about the permanent residents of Mount Hope. This nighttime walking tour of one of the oldest garden cemeteries in the country is a seasonal favorite.
<div>

Tours are conducted on foot and are no more than one mile, but may include stairs, hills, and uneven terrain. We recommend sturdy footwear, warm clothing, and a flashlight. Tours are conducted rain or shine.
<div>
Advanced Tickets are required and are sold for specific start times, starting at 6 pm.
<div>
<div>
Tickets will go on sale to the public on Thursday, September 24th, at noon.
<div>

Guests should enter Mount Hope Cemetery at 1048 State Street, Bangor, and check in near the Superintendent’s Lodge at no sooner than 20 minutes before their departure time. Parking is available along both sides of the cemetery entry road, accessible via the State Street gate.
<div>
Use “Second Maine Regiment Memorial” into GPS for the correct entrance gate location.
<div>
Direct questions to the museum curator via email at curator@bangorhistoricalsociety.org or by calling 207-942-1900.

The Bangor Historical Society’s Ghostly Bangor Walking Tour features tales of unsolved mysteries, murder, and energies that may still linger in the Queen City. Tours stroll through the streets of Downtown Bangor and last around 90 minutes. Tickets are $12.

Advanced ticketing is required. Our tours are capped at 25 guests, and tickets sell out quickly. Tickets must be purchased by noon of the date of the tour. To purchase tickets or for more info please visit our website or e-mail us at curator@bangorhistoricalsociety.org.
Tours depart from the Bangor Historical Society’s Thomas A. Hill House (159 Union Street, Bangor) at 7 p.m. Parking is available on High Street.

A note on inclement weather: tours will be cancelled if there is a chance of thunderstorms but not if only rain is in the forecast.

This three-part Teen Lab series gives teens the opportunity to see the creative process through from ideation to creation. They’ll get hands-on experience with printmaking by designing a pattern, carving linoleum, and making ink. Each part of the series will be led by a Walters Art Museum staff member who will answer questions from teens along the way about the creative process, printmaking, and working in a museum.
<ul>
• October 1:
Pattern Design with Elizabeth Norman, Assistant Manager of Gallery Experience & Interpretation
• November 5:
Linocut Reliefs with Adam Franchino, Lead Art Handler
• December 3:
Making Ink with Annette Ortiz, Conservation Scientist

Teen Lab is a space for teens to hang out, create art, and make friends. During this program, teens participate in creative activities, explore different cultures through art, and check out our galleries. Ages 13–18.
About the Staff

Elizabeth Norman is the Assistant Manager of Gallery Experience & Interpretation at the Walters Art Museum. Elizabeth writes interpretive text that you see in the museum’s galleries and the Build Your Own Tour Cards. She also leads the Express and Explore Tours, 30-minute art experiences that center around a different theme each month and allow participants to unplug and unwind in our galleries through playful activities. In her free time, Elizabeth is pursuing a personal art practice in relief printing.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

Let your generosity bloom! On Thursday, October 8, the Walters Art Museum is celebrating its fifth annual Day of Giving. To commemorate the 92nd birthday of our museum and its conservation lab, the third oldest in the country, we invite you to make a tangible impact on the objects in our collection that need urgent treatment and research.

This year, our conservators are hard at work restoring three beautiful 18th-century Sèvres porcelain vases. These delicate objects showcase incredible craftsmanship and imagination in both form and decoration. All three have suffered damage in the last two centuries and are currently undergoing repair in our conservation lab.

Donate now to help us preserve these objects and others like them today! Plus, when you make a gift now through October 8, your impact will be doubled thanks to a generous matching pledge. Every gift makes an impact and supports the work of the conservation team at the Walters.

In the summer of 2025, a technical study was conducted on six important 16th-century Limoges painted enamels at the Walters Art Museum, with surprising results. X-ray radiography, multispectral imaging, and microscopic examination identified previously unrecognized restorations- and shed light on a forgery now circulating on the international art market. Working in collaboration with curators and conservators at the Musee du Louvre, these sophisticated and deceptive restorations have been tied to the workshop of the talented 19th-century Parisian restorer and notorious forger Alfred André. Detailed drawings and notes recorded by André or his assistants between 1873 and 1909 reveal the restorer’s process and hint at how he created forgeries that continue to deceive today. Join Greg Bailey, Senior Objects Conservator, as he shares more about this interesting study.

The Walters Art Museum’s Conservation and Technical Research Department, founded in 1934, is the third oldest museum laboratory in the country. The Conservation Window provides visitors with an opportunity to see our conservators at work. Conservators engage with visitors while working on conservation-related projects in a small studio space adjacent to our labs, equipped with a window opening.

During all other museum hours, visitors can visit the window to see a display highlighting an in-progress conservation project. Whether you’re interested in art, science, history, or culture, we hope you will stop by, speak with our conservators, and learn something new about the Walters’ historic collection.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

Want to be part of Creative Alliance’s Great Baltimore Lantern and Dia de los Muertos Festival? This is your chance!

Throughout the month of October, the Walters Art Museum is offering lantern-making opportunities for visitors who wish to walk behind the Walters’ banner as we parade through Patterson Park. If you participated in one of these lantern-making events, you are invited to grab your lantern and join us. If you like, you can also create a lantern inspired by the Walters collection at home and walk alongside us.

Parade participants will meet at Patterson Park at 6:30 p.m. to assemble, and the parade will begin at 7 p.m. Registration is required so additional parade logistics can be provided via email.

All museum partners are invited to preview the museum’s fall exhibition, Luxury & Loss: Feather, Shell, Tusk, Horn, before it opens to the public. For centuries, artists around the world created luxurious objects from rare animal materials prized for their beauty and rarity. As understanding of the harm to wildlife grew, these materials were banned in the 20th century. Today, these objects help spark reflection, greater care for the natural world, and a more responsible relationship with nature.

This three-part Teen Lab series gives teens the opportunity to see the creative process through from ideation to creation. They’ll get hands-on experience with printmaking by designing a pattern, carving linoleum, and making ink. Each part of the series will be led by a Walters Art Museum staff member who will answer questions from teens along the way about the creative process, printmaking, and working in a museum.
<ul>
• October 1:
Pattern Design with Elizabeth Norman, Assistant Manager of Gallery Experience & Interpretation
• November 5:
Linocut Reliefs with Adam Franchino, Lead Art Handler
• December 3:
Making Ink with Annette Ortiz, Conservation Scientist

Teen Lab is a space for teens to hang out, create art, and make friends. During this program, teens participate in creative activities, explore different cultures through art, and check out our galleries. Ages 13-18.
About the Staff

As the museum’s Lead Art Handler, Adam Franchino transports art throughout the museum and builds mounts for artwork displays. In his spare time, Adam is also pursuing a personal art practice in printmaking.

The Walters Art Museum’s Conservation and Technical Research Department, founded in 1934, is the third oldest museum laboratory in the country. The Conservation Window provides visitors with an opportunity to see our conservators at work. Conservators engage with visitors while working on conservation-related projects in a small studio space adjacent to our labs, equipped with a window opening.

During all other museum hours, visitors can visit the window to see a display highlighting an in-progress conservation project. Whether you’re interested in art, science, history, or culture, we hope you will stop by, speak with our conservators, and learn something new about the Walters’ historic collection.

The Walters Art Museum’s Conservation and Technical Research Department, founded in 1934, is the third oldest museum laboratory in the country. The Conservation Window provides visitors with an opportunity to see our conservators at work. Conservators engage with visitors while working on conservation-related projects in a studio space adjacent to our labs, equipped with a window opening.

During all other museum hours, visitors can visit the window to see a display highlighting an in-progress conservation project. Whether you’re interested in art, science, history, or culture, we hope you will stop by, speak with our conservators, and learn something new about the Walters’ historic collection.

Tour participants should meet at Upper Charles Street entrance.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

What did luxury look like in the past? For hundreds of years, the powerful and the wealthy desired luxury that looked like iridescent kingfisher feathers, patterned tortoiseshells, creamy elephant ivories, and translucent rhinoceros horns. However, these extraction practices contributed to great losses in wildlife populations. And coupled with a growing environmental consciousness, governments around the world eventually banned the commercial trade of these wild animal materials starting in the 20th century. Join Dany Chan, Associate Curator of Asian Art and curator of the exhibition Luxury & Loss: Feather, Shell, Tusk, Horn, to examine the historical appeal of these four materials, the ecological impact of their uses, and society’s evolving responses to these past traditions, demonstrating an enduring human desire for beauty and luxury that still affects us today, both globally and in our own backyards.

The Walters Art Museum’s Conservation and Technical Research Department, founded in 1934, is the third oldest museum laboratory in the country. The Conservation Window provides visitors with an opportunity to see our conservators at work. Conservators engage with visitors while working on conservation-related projects in a small studio space adjacent to our labs, equipped with a window opening.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

Art and luxury goods made from wild animal materials testify to an enduring, human desire for beauty, but also to the harm to wild animal populations. The Walters Art Museum’s Education staff will explore with participants how the artworks on display convey society’s evolving relationship with nature and provide an opportunity for reflection and reconciliation.
During this workshop, you will…
<ul>
• Engage in a guided tour of our special exhibition Luxury and Loss: Feather, Shell, Tusk, Horn
• Create your own work of art
• Connect and build community with other educators
• Learn about free tours and opportunities for you and your students at the Walters

This event is for teachers, administrators, support staff, and informal educators.

This three-part Teen Lab series gives teens the opportunity to see the creative process through from ideation to creation. They’ll get hands-on experience with printmaking by designing a pattern, carving linoleum, and making ink. Each part of the series will be led by a Walters Art Museum staff member who will answer questions from teens along the way about the creative process, printmaking, and working in a museum.
<ul>
• October 1:
Pattern Design with Elizabeth Norman, Assistant Manager of Gallery Experience & Interpretation
• November 5:
Linocut Reliefs with Adam Franchino, Lead Art Handler
• December 3:
Making Ink with Annette Ortiz, Conservation Scientist

Teen Lab is a space for teens to hang out, create art, and make friends. During this program, teens participate in creative activities, explore different cultures through art, and check out our galleries. Ages 13-18.
About the Staff

As the museum’s Conservation Scientist, Annette Ortiz examines Earth and mineral pigments in their raw forms to learn about the paints used in paintings and sculptures.

Art and luxury goods made from wild animal materials testify to an enduring, human desire for their beauty, but also to the consequential harm to wild animal populations. Join Dany Chan, Associate Curator of Asian Art, in Luxury & Loss: Feather, Shell, Tusk, Horn to examine the historical appeal, ecological impact, and the evolving responses to art made with kingfisher feathers, tortoiseshell, rhinoceros horn, and elephant ivory.

Tour participants should meet in the Centre Street Lobby.

The Walters Art Museum is a cultural hub in the heart of Baltimore. Located in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, the Walters is free for all. The museum’s collection spans more than seven millennia, from 5,000 BCE to the 21st century, and encompasses 36,000 objects from around the world.

\n

Walking through the museum’s historic buildings, visitors encounter a stunning panorama of thousands of years of art, from romantic 19th-century images of French gardens to mesmerizing Ethiopian icons, richly illuminated Qur’ans and Gospel books, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and serene images of the Buddha.

The Walters Art Museum’s Conservation and Technical Research Department, founded in 1934, is the third oldest museum laboratory in the country. The Conservation Window provides visitors with an opportunity to see our conservators at work. Conservators engage with visitors while working on conservation-related projects in a small studio space adjacent to our labs, equipped with a window opening.

La Pachanga
Live Music by Marlow Rosado
Set by DJ Danis La Clave
21+ with ID

La Pachanga is Ball & Chain’s Saturday night main event: a live Latin music party that takes over the patio, the stage, and eventually the entire building. The night opens with DJ sets that build the room, then the live band hits and the dancing starts. You will hear salsa, timba, Latin jazz, and whatever else the performers feel like throwing in. The lineup rotates, but the energy doesn’t.

La Pachanga runs every Saturday from 9pm to 3am. No cover charge. No bottle service required. Just show up (though we encourage you to RSVP!).

Salsero Sundays
Sets by DJ Vila
Free Salsa Class at 9:00pm
21+ with ID

Every Sunday night, Ball & Chain brings the heart of Little Havana to life with Salsero Sundays, one of Miami’s most popular weekly Latin dance nights. Located on iconic Calle Ocho, Salsero Sundays combines live DJ sets, salsa dancing, handcrafted cocktails, the best Cuban food in Miami,  and the unmistakable energy that has made Ball & Chain a legendary destination for decades.

BachaTuesdays at Ball & Chain
Set by DJ Vila
Free Bachata Class at 9pm

BachaTuesdays is the night Ball & Chain hands over to bachata. The room shifts when the music does, and the room knows the difference. By 8:30 the patio crowd is finishing dinner and the floor is starting to settle into the night. By 9pm, Sensual Movement is running the free bachata class for whoever wants to learn, and the night’s DJ is queuing up the bachata sets that go until 1am.

Ball & Chain presents
La Pachanga
Live Music by Julio Montalvo y el Huracan de Miami
Set by DJ Danis La Clave
21+ with ID

La Pachanga is Ball & Chain’s Saturday night main event: a live Latin music party that takes over the patio, the stage, and eventually the entire building. The night opens with DJ sets that build the room, then the live band hits and the dancing starts. You will hear salsa, timba, Latin jazz, and whatever else the performers feel like throwing in. The lineup rotates, but the energy doesn’t.

La Pachanga is every Saturday from 9pm to 3am. No cover charge. No bottle service required. Just show up (though we encourage you to RSVP!).
